title: This world as practice
hookLine: many teachers say the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure here

cards: Shariputra had a worry, and in the Vimalakirti Sutra he keeps it to himself. If a buddha's land is pure when his mind is pure, he wonders, then why does this world look the way it does?
Hills and pits, thorns and gravel, dirt and mess. The Buddha hears the thought anyway. He presses the ground with his toe, and for a moment the whole world shows itself covered in jewels.
Then he says, more or less: it was always like this. You just weren't seeing it. Today: this world as practice.

teach.h: AS THE MIND IS PURE, THE LAND IS PURE.
teach.b: First, the line that sets it up.
Just before that scene, the Vimalakirti Sutra has the Buddha say, in effect, that a bodhisattva who wants a pure land should purify the mind, because as the mind is purified, the land is purified.

Some teachers in East Asia read the Pure Land sutras with that line in their ear. The land of bliss in the west is real to them, and it also points at something closer: a mind made pure, here. Second, the toe.
Shariputra wasn't wrong about the gravel. The sutra doesn't say the thorns are imaginary.
It says the same ground looks different depending on who is looking. The work isn't to move somewhere cleaner. It's to see this place clearly.

teach.h: AN OLDER ECHO: PURIFY ONE'S MIND.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, sums up the teaching in one breath: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
Purifying the mind isn't a Pure Land invention; it sits in a verse that says nothing about a land in the west. Fourth, what this looks like on a Tuesday. A pure mind, here, isn't a spotless mind.
It's a moment met without the extra layer: the grudge, the rush, the story about how this shouldn't be happening. Washing a pan without resenting it. Answering a message without the sharp edge.
For these teachers, that small clean moment is a glimpse of the land itself.
Tomorrow: how Pure Land teachers answer differently about where the land really is.

how: Some Pure Land and Chan teachers in East Asia pair calling Amitabha's name with the teaching, from the Vimalakirti Sutra, that as the mind is purified the land is purified, so daily life itself becomes a place of practice.

games.q: what does “this world as practice” mean?
o: a mind made pure here, so ordinary ground is practice
a vow to clean and repair temples as a daily duty
a teaching that this world is a dream to escape from

games.q: this world as practice: tap the pairs.
p: wondered why this world looks so rough
showed the world covered in jewels

s: in the sutra, the thorns and gravel are only imaginary
the sutra says the same ground looks different depending on who is looking.
purifying the mind appears in the Dhammapada too
"to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened," in Max Müller's translation.
a pure mind means a spotless mind with no thoughts
here it means a moment met without the extra layer of grudge or rush.

games.q: you're Shariputra. this world looks full of thorns and gravel, and you wonder why. the Buddha presses the ground with his toe. what does he show you?
o: a cleaner world somewhere else, to move to.
this same world, covered in jewels.
that the thorns were never there.
games.why: the world shows itself covered in jewels, and the Buddha says it was always like this. the change is in the seeing, not the place.

practice: When the next small moment comes, a sip of water, a step, a breath, do just that one thing, with nothing added: no commentary, no hurry, no complaint. Then do it again with the next one.
If a grudge or a worry slips in, notice it, and let the next breath be clean.

wordCard.voice: This world as practice. The teaching that the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure right here, so ordinary ground becomes the place of practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: buddhakshetra, a buddha-field, the land around a buddha. Sukhavati is Amitabha's.

carryVoice: Your line: pure here. The same ground, seen clearly. See you tomorrow.
